transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood CSM), Evan (BlueHarbor CTO), Sarah (Head of MLOps), Rahul (Platform)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): QBR-style checkin covering costs and reliability, looking to run a dedicated PoC and dig into 99p latency. Action items captured.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time — quick check, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Evan: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:06] Sarah: Good here.
[00:08] Maya: Great. We're set for about 50 minutes, quick agenda: walk April usage/costs, dig into the 99th percentile latency spikes you flagged, talk options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), then security/retention items, and close with next steps. Sound good?
[00:20] Rahul: Sounds good, want to start with the cost thing. April was weird.
[00:24] Maya: Yeah, Jordan and I looked at the bill — there was a big uptick in embedding ops and a handful of long-context generation tails late nights. Jordan, do you want to take the numbers?
[00:33] Jordan: Sure. So, rough top-line: BlueHarbor's hosted usage tokens were up ~28% MoM, but the cost increased ~46% due to two drivers: one, more requests hitting the long context path (we saw more 8k+ sequences), and two, an increase in quantization fallback — a small percentage of model shards routed to the higher-precision variant during bursts. We have the per-model breakdown and the sample traces.
[00:53] Sarah: A quick clarifying question — when you say "quantization fallback", is that the model switching to float16 on the hot path? We didn't expect that.
[00:58] Jordan: Right, so our runtime will occasionally route to a compatible but higher-cost variant when the faster quantized kernel can't satisfy the sequence length or memory pattern. It's an automatic safety path to avoid OOM and to keep latency low, but it costs more.
[01:12] Evan: Ok, that explains the cost delta then. Any idea why we had more long sequences in April? We didn't change the product.
[01:18] Priya: We looked at campaign logs — you had two promotion windows last month, longer contextual prompts from commerce flows — also some partners passing full session history which increased prefix lengths.
[01:27] Rahul: Yeah, the affiliate widget started storing user context for personalization, that increased average tokens per request. We own that change.
[01:32] Maya: Useful context — so part product change, part runtime behavior. The good news is we can take both tactical and strategic steps: tactical — suggest batching tweaks and prefix caching; strategic — consider dedicated pool + quantized model variants pinned to you.
[01:45] Sarah: Can we get numbers on how much dedicated capacity would cut per-token costs? We're sensitive to margin.
[01:50] Jordan: Absolutely. From our model: dedicated GPUs with pinned quantized model variants and KV caching could reduce effective per-token cost by ~25-40% depending on utilization and batching. We'll send a model-by-model sheet.
[02:03] Evan: That sounds promising, but we need proof for worst-case latency. We can't have promo windows with 99p spikes.
[02:10] Jordan: Totally. On the latency front we see reproducible 99th percent spikes around promo windows — usually coinciding with sudden bursts that push routing into the safety fallbacks and flush some KV caches. The traces show increased queueing time and then a handful of tails where the request hits a non-quantized path.
[02:27] Rahul: I can share our synthetic prom load tests, but we want real traces from you as well to compare.
[02:30] Jordan: We'll extract 95/99p traces and the queue length histograms for the April windows and share raw logs. That should help pinpoint whether it's routing, batching, or cold-KV misses.
[02:39] Sarah: Also curious about cold starts for your dedicated pool — are there warmers?
[02:43] Maya: Dedicated lets you keep pinned warm replicas; autoscaling can be tuned but with reserved capacity you avoid cold starts. For burst capacity we have policies that can temporarily spin additional instances but that reintroduces some warm-up latency — tradeoff.
[02:56] Evan: Ok. Let's talk about the PoC: what's a realistic scope and timeline if we want to validate cost and 99p latency under our peak?
[03:03] Jordan: Typical timeline: provision dedicated pool in staging, run three load patterns (baseline, promo spike, partner session replay), measure cost and latency and KV hit-rate. We can do that in a 2–3 week window assuming staging credentials and sample traffic. Success criteria we recommend: 99p latency below X ms (we'll propose concrete number), cost per 1M tokens reduced by Y%, and KV cache hit-rate > 85%.
[03:23] Rahul: Can we define X and Y? We need clear SLOs for our ops team.
[03:27] Jordan: Yes — we'll propose a baseline 99p SLO of 450ms for your current models (we'll tune after we see traces) and a cost reduction target of 30% as an initial estimate. We'll make those configurable in the PoC doc.
[03:39] Priya: I'll attach a draft PoC plan after the call with milestones and measurement dashboards.
[03:44] Maya: Great. Switching to security: you had a question about KMS audit trails and retention — Priya, do you want to take that?
[03:50] Priya: Sure. BlueHarbor asked if Redwood stores any customer keys — short answer is no, we integrate with customer KMS for private deployments and for Dedicated we offer options: customer-managed KMS or Redwood-managed with strict key rotation. For hosted, we have encryption at rest and envelope encryption, but we can provide SOC2 excerpts and audit trail samples.
[04:10] Sarah: We specifically need to show auditors that key usage events are logged with a traceable ID and retention is configurable to 7 years.
[04:17] Priya: We'll surface the KMS audit schema and retention options; for the hosted API we can show the relevant fields we log. For Dedicated/Private we can map to your KMS provider — if you need 7 years retention, that's doable with an agreed contract addendum.
[04:30] Evan: Good. Any issues with data residency for EU tenants? Not critical for us but want to confirm.
[04:36] Jordan: We have region pinning for model serving, and you can pin to EU regions for both hosted and Dedicated. Private on-prem eliminates residency concerns.
[04:43] Rahul: One more security note: our internal compliance team wants to check the ability to redact PII in logs and request bodies — how feasible?
[04:50] Priya: We support log redaction rules and can apply regex-based scrubbing for fields; we also have a data retention policy and can redact at the ingestion point. We'll share examples.
[04:58] Sarah: Thanks, that helps.
[05:02] Maya: Back to performance — Jordan, could you explain the KV cache strategy and why we saw misses during the promo windows?
[05:08] Jordan: Sure. Our KV cache is prefix-based and sized by working set. During promo bursts, more unique prefixes appear (because of session history and partner parameters) which reduces hit-rate. Also, when we route to fallback variants the cache addressing can differ slightly, leading to apparent misses. We saw hit-rate drop from ~88% to ~60% in the busiest 10-minute windows.
[05:25] Rahul: So we should either reduce prefix size or increase cache footprint? Which is lower risk?
[05:29] Jordan: Increasing cache footprint in Dedicated is easiest and lowest risk; prefix trimming needs product work. There's also an approach to normalize partner session keys at the middleware so you're not generating unique prefixes for identical user intents.
[05:41] Evan: I like the normalization idea but it's heavier lift. For the quick win we'll try dedicated cache increase during promos.
[05:47] Maya: We'll quantify the delta — Jordan will propose cache sizing and the cost impact.
[05:51] Sarah: On billing, we also noticed some opaque line items labeled "safety fallthrough" — can you clarify?
[05:58] Jordan: That's the cost of routing to a higher-precision variant as I mentioned. It's labeled in the bill as fallthrough. We'll annotate the April invoice and mark which line items correspond to that.
[06:10] Rahul: Sounds good.
[06:12] Maya: Quick mid-call recap — agreed items: Jordan to pull latency traces and queue histograms; Maya to send per-model cost breakdown and annotate fallthrough costs; Priya to send SOC2/KMS artifacts; Rahul to provision staging creds for the PoC. Anything missing?
[06:25] Evan: No, that's fair.
[06:27] Priya: I'll add PoC milestones and dashboards.
[06:31] Sarah: A small ask — can you include comparisons to competitors? We're evaluating ModelServe and CloudPrompt as well.
[06:36] Maya: We can provide a high-level comparison deck focusing on cost and SLOs. We'll keep it objective.
[06:42] Jordan: One more technical pointer — you may get better tail behavior if you cap the maximum sequence length at the application layer and use summarization to compress history. That reduces long-context tails without heavy infra changes.
[06:53] Rahul: We'll test a small branch to cap the prefix. That might be easiest.
[06:57] Maya: Cool. Any other performance deep-dive items?
[07:00] Sarah: Did you notice any correlation between specific model versions and spikes? We try to pin to stable branches.
[07:05] Jordan: Yes — during April some traffic hit a 2.1 variant which had different kernel shapes that triggered more fallbacks under certain batch sizes. We recommend pinning to the 2.0 quantized variant for the PoC and only roll 2.1 after validation.
[07:18] Evan: Noted.
[07:20] Maya: Ok shifting to timeline and business case — what's the rough cost to spin a dedicated PoC for 3 weeks?
[07:26] Jordan: For a staging-sized pool tuned to your peak we estimate a commitment of about $7k-$12k for the short PoC depending on whether you want burst-capacity enabled. We'll give a firm quote in the follow-up.
[07:36] Evan: Budget's doable if the results show 30% cost reduction.
[07:40] Priya: We'll include expected ROI calculations in the cost sheet so you can present to finance.
[07:45] Rahul: On the PoC data flow — will logs include full request text? We might want masked logs.
[07:50] Jordan: Logs can be masked/redacted per your policy; for latency traces we can provide hashed request IDs and timing without full payload if that's preferred.
[07:58] Sarah: Please do masked by default.
[08:00] Maya: Noted.
[08:02] Evan: Any blockers from Redwood's side to run the PoC?
[08:05] Jordan: Just staging credentials and a small sample of partner session format. We can provision the dedicated pool in our staging region in ~3 business days once we have that.
[08:13] Rahul: I'll get those creds and sample session data by Tuesday.
[08:16] Maya: Great.
[08:18] Priya: On compliance, we'll also propose contract language for KMS retention and SOC2 addendum for the dedicated deployment.
[08:26] Sarah: Thanks.
[08:28] Maya: We're at about 35 minutes in — want to run quick Q&A and then recap.
[08:32] Evan: Two quick questions: one on monitoring — can we tie your per-route dashboards into our Grafana?
[08:37] Jordan: Yes, we provide Prometheus metrics and can export via remote write, or we can set up a webhook-based integration. We'll provide the metric names and an example dashboard.
[08:46] Sarah: Second question — post-PoC, if results are good, what's the ramp path to Dedicated in production?
[08:51] Maya: You can either convert staging pool settings to production reserved capacity with a commit, or run a gradual rollout by pinning a percentage of traffic to Dedicated and expanding. We support canary and A/B routing.
[09:02] Evan: Sounds good.
[09:04] Maya: Any other questions?
[09:06] Rahul: One housekeeping — please put all artifacts in the CRM deal folder so our procurement can see them.
[09:11] Priya: Will do.
[09:13] Maya: Ok final recap and next steps: 1) Maya send model-by-model cost breakdown and annotate April fallthroughs (due 2027-05-14); 2) Jordan export latency traces and queue histograms (due 2027-05-20); 3) Rahul provision staging creds and sample sessions (due 2027-05-18); 4) Priya attach SOC2 excerpt and KMS audit schema (due 2027-05-16); 5) schedule 2hr PoC kickoff once staging creds are in place (suggest week of 2027-05-24).
[09:46] Evan: That's clear. Thanks all.
[09:49] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with an email and the PoC doc. Bye.
[09:54] Sarah: Bye.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker attributions are mostly correct but timestamps are approximate; some technical terms like "KV cache" and "quantized kernel" occasionally transcribed inconsistently (e.g., "quantization fallthrough"/"fallback").
